title: Harvard Study: Claude Code Productivity Gains Vanish
description: Harvard's 718-firm study found AI agents raise coding output 30% but firm output stays flat. Code review is the bottleneck. What the data actually says.
author: freellm.site
content:
The Harvard study everyone is arguing about does **not** say Claude Code fails to make engineers more productive. At the individual level it finds the opposite: AI agents raise code output by about 30%. What it then finds is that the gain doesn't show up in shipped software or headcount, because code review absorbs it. Review time per pull request rises 49%, the share of PRs that get a formal change request nearly doubles, and firms pull 14% more workers into reviewing.

![Harvard Study: Claude Code Productivity Gains Vanish](/images/blog/harvard-claude-code-productivity-study/image-0.jpg)

The paper is [*Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production*](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf) by Fiona Chen and James Stratton (Harvard). The first version appeared in January 2026 and the current version is dated August 4, 2026. If you came from a thread titled "no increase in productivity from using Claude Code," that title compresses the abstract and drops the first half of the sentence.

## What the study measured

This isn't a lab experiment with 16 developers. It uses a proprietary dataset from Jellyfish, an engineering analytics platform, covering roughly 300 million work events from about 726,000 workers across 718 firms, from January 2021 through March 2026. The data combines five sources: HR records, version control (GitHub), issue tracking (Jira), calendars (Google Calendar), and AI tool usage for GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code.

The design is a staggered difference-in-differences on **firm-level** adoption timing. That matters for reading the numbers: the treatment is "your company bought the tool," not "you personally used it today." Worker-level take-up is partial (the paper reports the median firm reaching roughly 20% agent adoption among engineers by month 12, and top-quintile firms around 60%), so the effect sizes average over users and non-users. The authors note that this is why their estimates sit at the lower end of comparable work.

The paper splits tools into two generations:

- **AI assistants**: inline completion and chat, such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor.
- **AI agents**: semi-autonomous, multi-step tools such as Claude Code, Cursor Agent, Devin and Copilot Agent, detected through API data plus GitHub bot accounts and commit signatures.

Firm adoption of agents went from near zero in October 2024 to over 95% by January 2026, accelerating most sharply around the Cursor Agent and Claude Code releases.

## The results, in one table

| Outcome | AI assistants | AI agents |
|---|---|---|
| Lines of code added | +12% (not significant) | **+30%** |
| Commits | +9% (significant) | **+20%** |
| Pull requests | +5% (not significant) | **+23%** |
| Jira issues / epics resolved | small, not significant | small, not significant (rules out >12%) |
| Overall employment | precise zero | precise zero (rules out >2.9% decline) |
| PR time-to-merge | no significant effect | **+49%** (+3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline) |
| Share of PRs with changes requested | +0.01 (not significant) | **+0.12 on a 0.13 baseline** (nearly double) |
| Review comments per PR | no significant effect | **+0.58 on a 1.66 baseline** (+35%) |
| Share of workers doing code review | +10% | **+14%** (0.29 baseline) |
| Share of workers writing code | no significant change | no significant change |

Two things stand out. Assistants barely move anything except commits, so the Copilot-era gains were small at the firm level. And agents move every upstream measure a lot while leaving downstream measures untouched.

## "But I'm shipping 3x the tickets." Are you wrong?

No, and the study agrees with you. The most upvoted correction in the Reddit threads got it right: individual coding productivity goes up. If you close several tickets a day where you used to close a few a week, you're a data point inside that +30%.

The paper adds what you can't see from your own desk. Your extra pull requests land in someone else's queue. Firm-level Jira issue resolution, which only ticks when code is deployed, doesn't move. The authors also checked the obvious objection that issues got bigger: they used ML to predict how long each issue should take an engineer and found no effect on average predicted issue length. They separately checked whether PRs got bigger and found no significant change in lines added per PR (baseline ~1,168 lines). So the review slowdown isn't caused by chunkier work.

![Engineer reviewing a long code diff on a monitor with a queue of pending pull requests](/images/blog/harvard-claude-code-productivity-study/image-1.jpg)
*Photo: [Developer Satisfaction Survey - 2020 - Code Review - important to work](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=90638476) by Greg (WMF), CC BY-SA*

## "Coding was never the bottleneck" was the correct comment

That comment earned its upvotes. The paper estimates how engineers spend their time from the Jellyfish signals and gets 42% writing code; a validation survey of 100 engineers on Prolific puts it at 30%. Call it 30 to 40%.

If you make a third of the job twice as fast and leave the other two-thirds alone, Amdahl's law caps your gain hard, and that assumes the other two-thirds don't get *worse*. Here they do. The authors' model formalizes this: AI changes two things at once, coding productivity `A(t)` and the bug rate of draft code `π(t)`. Higher `A` on its own would raise good output. Higher `π` raises the review effort needed per unit of code and reduces how much good software ships. More code, longer reviews, more change requests and flat deploys are exactly what you see when both effects happen and review labour can't be reassigned instantly.

The paper also quotes a junior engineer describing how this plays out: huge commit volume, one senior engineer gatekeeping a codebase, weekly review slots, and then new rules after outages requiring senior approval specifically for AI-generated code. The review bottleneck got worse in its structure, not just in queue length.

## "Just have Claude review its own code." Firms already tried, at scale

The joke answer in the thread is what firms actually did, and the paper measured it. By March 2026, nearly 80% of firms had used AI tools in code review (the authors detected CodeRabbit, Greptile, Copilot Reviewer, Cursor Bug Bot, Graphite and Bito).

It didn't clear the bottleneck. Only **23.3%** of review comments are AI-generated, and only **10.8%** of pull requests get even one AI-generated comment. The authors say plainly that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt AI review tools, because humans remain central to review. A senior engineer they interviewed gives the reason: the tools don't understand what the whole feature is supposed to do.

That's an argument from structure, not impressions. Checking work you didn't do requires knowing its intent, and the intent is what a diff shows least. The same gap appears in [AI engineer interviews, where testing AI-assisted coding means testing review judgment](/blog/ai-engineer-interview-ai-assisted-coding/), and it's what makes [liability for autonomous agents](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/) hard to assign.

## What about layoffs?

The employment result gets the least coverage. For AI agents, the estimate for overall employment is a precise zero, tight enough to rule out a decline larger than 2.9%. For engineering employment specifically it's a noisier zero, ruling out a decline larger than 13.8%. Neither fits a 30% coding productivity gain passing through fully into job cuts.

The share of workers writing code didn't fall either. What changed is that *more* people now also review. Work moved toward verification instead of disappearing.

## Measure your own bottleneck before you argue about it

The paper's advice to managers: intermediate metrics like lines of code and commits will show a win that may not exist downstream, so measure time-to-merge and change-request rate instead. Here's a runnable script that pulls those two numbers for your own repo from the GitHub REST API, with no dependencies beyond `requests`.

```python
import os, statistics, requests
from datetime import datetime, timezone

REPO = "owner/name"              # change me
TOKEN = os.environ["GITHUB_TOKEN"]
H = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
     "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json"}

def merged_prs(repo, pages=5):
    for page in range(1, pages + 1):
        r = requests.get(
            f"https://api.github.com/repos/{repo}/pulls",
            headers=H,
            params={"state": "closed", "per_page": 100,
                    "page": page, "sort": "updated"},
            timeout=30,
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        batch = r.json()
        if not batch:
            return
        for pr in batch:
            if pr.get("merged_at"):
                yield pr

def hours(a, b):
    fmt = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
    t0 = datetime.strptime(a, fmt).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    t1 = datetime.strptime(b, fmt).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    return (t1 - t0).total_seconds() / 3600

lags, changes_requested, total = [], 0, 0
for pr in merged_prs(REPO):
    total += 1
    lags.append(hours(pr["created_at"], pr["merged_at"]))
    rev = requests.get(
        f"https://api.github.com/repos/{REPO}/pulls/{pr['number']}/reviews",
        headers=H, timeout=30,
    ).json()
    if any(x.get("state") == "CHANGES_REQUESTED" for x in rev):
        changes_requested += 1

print(f"merged PRs analysed:      {total}")
print(f"median time-to-merge:     {statistics.median(lags)/24:.2f} days")
print(f"p90 time-to-merge:        {statistics.quantiles(lags, n=10)[-1]/24:.2f} days")
print(f"changes-requested rate:   {changes_requested/total:.1%}")
```

Run it on a window before your agent rollout and a window after. If median time-to-merge went up and the changes-requested rate jumped, you're reproducing the paper on your own repo, and the fix is more review capacity and smaller PRs, not a better model.

## Practical read for engineers and managers

- **Don't report commits or LOC as an AI win.** The paper's own numbers show those rise while deploys don't. Track issue/epic resolution and time-to-merge.
- **Budget review capacity when you roll out agents.** The firms in the data did move people toward review (+14% of workers), and the model shows that *without* that shift, even less of the gain reaches shipped software.
- **Smaller PRs are the cheapest fix.** Review effort per unit of code rises with the bug rate, and big agent-generated diffs pile that cost onto one reviewer.
- **Keep a human checking intent.** Nearly every firm has adopted AI review tools, and they still write under a quarter of review comments. Use them as a first pass on mechanics.
- **Separate tool choice from process choice.** Model quality isn't what's limiting throughput here. To experiment cheaply while you fix the process, see [the best free LLM APIs for coding in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-for-coding/) or [how to wire a free API into Cursor or Claude Code](/blog/use-free-llm-api-cursor-claude-code/).

The authors flag one caveat themselves. The method assumes early and late adopters would have followed parallel paths without adoption. They test balance, find that larger firms adopt earlier, and add time-varying firm-size controls. The AI assistant specification shows differential pre-trends in engineering employment, which they say makes that particular estimate ambiguous. The agent results, which this article is about, are the cleaner half.

## FAQ

### Does the Harvard study say Claude Code makes developers less productive?

No. It finds that AI agents increase individual coding productivity: +30% lines of code, +20% commits and +23% pull requests, all statistically significant. The finding is that this doesn't carry through to firm-level software output or employment.

### Why doesn't the extra code turn into shipped features?

Code review becomes the bottleneck. Time from PR open to merge rises 49% (3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline), the share of PRs with a formal change request nearly doubles from 0.13, and comments per PR rise 35%. PRs didn't get bigger, so larger diffs don't explain the slowdown.

### Do AI code review tools solve the bottleneck?

Not according to the data. Nearly 80% of firms had used AI in code review by March 2026, yet only 23.3% of review comments are AI-generated and only 10.8% of PRs get even one. The paper says the bottleneck persists after adoption because humans remain central to review.

### Did AI coding agents cause engineering layoffs in this dataset?

There's no measurable effect. The estimate for overall employment is a precise zero, ruling out a decline greater than 2.9%; for engineering employment it's a noisier zero that rules out more than a 13.8% decline. Work shifted toward review instead of shrinking.

### How is this different from earlier Copilot studies?

It measures firm-level adoption across 718 companies instead of individual task performance, and it tracks the whole pipeline from commits through Jira deployment. The closest earlier work (Demirer, Musolff & Yang, 2026) found a similar incomplete pass-through for Copilot on open-source repos. For exact methodology, effect sizes and caveats, read the paper itself; no blog summary, including this one, is a substitute.
